title: Teach Us to Care and Not to Care
author: Restarting School
summary: This is an author's introduction and excerpt from a new book on classroom assessment, drawing an unusual analogy between an elderly Japanese hobbyist who creates fine art in Microsoft Excel and the way schools handle grading: both involve unlikely tools that can be used well or overused into misery. The author argues that assessment practices like zeroes, rigid deadlines, and punitive grading policies could have the same beneficial qualities Excel-art has for its creator, entertainment, beauty, usefulness, but instead schools frequently overdo these tools until they become sources of stress for students and teachers alike, quoting Chesterton's line about thanking God for beer and Burgundy by not drinking too much of them. The book situates itself alongside established assessment reformers Rick Wormeli, Rick Stiggins, and Douglas Reeves, sharing many of their practical recommendations (retakes, flexible deadlines, the importance of hope in grading) while explicitly diverging from their progressive-education framing in favor of arguments grounded in older sources and economic-style incentive thinking. The author's larger claim is that teachers across very different philosophical traditions, classical, progressive, homeschool, and STEM-centered alike, can converge on the same practical fixes to grading even while disagreeing about the underlying philosophy, because the shared problem (a student buried under mathematically unrecoverable zeroes) is visible regardless of ideological starting point.
points: The book's central move is arguing that assessment tools (deadlines, zeroes, rubrics) are morally neutral instruments that produce misery only through overuse, using Tatsuo Horiuchi's Excel-art hobby as an analogy for a tool used with restraint and enjoyment.

It deliberately draws on the same practical toolkit as Wormeli, Stiggins, and Reeves (retakes, flexible deadlines, hope in grading) while explicitly rejecting their progressive-education philosophical framing in favor of 'older sources' and economic-incentive reasoning.

The author's key claim about cross-tradition convergence, that classical, progressive, and homeschool educators can agree assessment isn't working even while disagreeing about why, positions the book as a philosophically ecumenical practical guide rather than a partisan one.

The specific disagreement flagged with prior reformers (on zeroes, retake friction, and where boundaries should sit) signals the book takes tactical, not wholesale, issue with the existing grading-reform literature.

The title's source in T.S. Eliot's 'Ash Wednesday' frames assessment as requiring a disciplined balance between caring enough to hold standards and not caring so much that the system becomes punitive.
quotes: But instead of seeing how we might make assessments interesting, or entertaining, or even, like Horiuchi has done with Excel, beautiful, we take these things that we complain about, and then overdo our uses of them.

To quote G.K. Chesterton, "We should thank God for beer and Burgundy by not drinking too much of them." It takes a brave teacher or school leader to use assessment in the right ways, at the right times, and in moderation.

Wormeli, Stiggins, and Reeves all write from within the progressive education tradition, emphasizing differentiation, equity, and formative feedback systems. The arguments in this book draw instead on older sources and on economic-style incentives.

A localist who believes in civil society, small institutions, and economic incentives, and a progressive differentiation advocate can look at a student buried under mathematically unrecoverable zeroes and a teacher trying to do her best for the students but hemmed in by conventions and policy and agree: this is not working.

Teachers in conventional public and private schools, in classical schools, in project-based or STEM-centered schools, in Charlotte Mason schools, in hybrid homeschools or microschools of all kinds will be able to take ideas from this book and apply them in their own contexts.
